paras: The lynching of Jack Williams took place early on October 13, 1881, when a crowd took Williams, a Black man, from the jail at Orangeburg, South Carolina, and hanged him from a tree on the edge of town. Williams had been convicted days earlier of assaulting an eleven-year-old white girl, but the jury's recommendation to mercy meant a sentence of life imprisonment instead of death. The papers stressed that the crowd overrode a completed trial, and much of the South Carolina press approved.

At the October court term in Orangeburg County, Williams was convicted on Saturday, October 8, of an "outrageous assault" on Linnie Hughes, a white girl living a few miles from town. Reports gave her age as eleven, though one copy of the same dispatch said fourteen and others twelve or seven. The jury found him guilty but recommended him to mercy, which under state law fixed the punishment at life in the penitentiary, and Judge Hudson sentenced him accordingly on Wednesday, October 12.

According to the Newberry Herald, there had been threats of lynching before the trial, but because conviction and hanging seemed certain "it was agreed to let the law take its course." Ten of the twelve jurors then handed the judge a paper saying they had believed the court could still impose death; it was not read or acted on.

About 2 a.m. on Thursday, October 13, a drunken man was brought to the guardhouse inside the jail, and when the door was opened for him a crowd rushed in and overpowered the jailer. Accounts of the crowd differ: "a large crowd of citizens" to the News and Courier's correspondent, about twenty-five men "from the scene of the outrage" in a Charleston dispatch, and 150 masked persons who overpowered the Sheriff in the Keowee Courier. They carried Williams to the suburbs, on the road across the Edisto River about a quarter mile from the jail, and hanged him from a tree limb.

The correspondent "understood" that Williams had confessed after his trial and again that night, and the Charleston dispatch said the crowd obtained a repeated confession. Fastened across the breast of the body was a piece of white homespun printed in large letters: "Our wives, mothers, sisters and daughters shall be protected, the decision of an Orangeburg jury to the contrary notwithstanding." The body was taken down about noon.

The Orangeburg correspondent reported "little or no excitement," and the Charleston dispatch said some were surprised the jurors had not also been executed. No report of an inquest, of any arrest of the lynchers or of action on the jurors' paper appears in the coverage.

The fullest account was a special dispatch to the Charleston News and Courier signed "Hermes," which the Fairfield News and Herald reprinted under the headline "The Law of Self-Preservation." The Abbeville Press and Banner ran the same dispatch as "A Case of Justifiable Lynching," writing that "No good citizen could condemn the act," and the Pickens Sentinel's "A Just Retribution" said of the lynchers, "They did right, and we commend their act." The Savannah Morning News headed its Charleston dispatch "Innocence Avenged" and "A Stupid Jury's Work Completed."

More guarded, the Keowee Courier called the hanging a just retribution but regretted it was not done "under and by the law," and the Anderson Intelligencer called it "a defiance of law" that public opinion would nonetheless not condemn, putting the blame on the jury. The one condemnation found came from the Baptist Courier in Columbia, which did not dispute Williams's guilt but wrote that lynching "is nothing less than murder" and called for a law to punish lynchers. In Charlotte, the Home and Democrat used the case to argue for jury reform.

Outside the state, an Associated Press dispatch from Charleston ran on October 14 and 15 from Memphis and Washington to St. Paul and Bismarck. Its headlines included "Negro Hanged by a Mob," "Mob Law in South Carolina" and "An Objectionable Verdict Corrected," and the Bismarck Tribune wrote that a mob had reversed "the popular Verdict of a Jury." Wire copies called the girl "Lizzie," some condensed versions put the hanging in the afternoon, and weeklies reprinted the item through late October.

reader.title: Lynching of Jack Williams
bases: A crowd took Williams, a convicted Black prisoner, from the Orangeburg jail and hanged him (A19, A4, A23).

A crowd variously put at about 25 men and at 150 took Williams from jail without lawful authority and hanged him, to secure the death sentence a jury's mercy recommendation had ruled out (A4, A23, A19); a placard said it was done to protect 'our wives, mothers, sisters and daughters' (A19).

The News and Courier's Orangeburg dispatch, the AP Charleston wire, a separate Charleston dispatch and independent South Carolina accounts all agree that a crowd took Williams from the jail and hanged him (A19, A6, A4, A24, A23).

framing.detail: The Abbeville Press and Banner headed the dispatch 'A Case of Justifiable Lynching' and wrote that 'the people of Orangeburg did right'.
The Pickens Sentinel's 'A Just Retribution' commended the lynchers: 'They did right, and we commend their act.'
The Savannah Morning News headed its dispatch 'Innocence Avenged' and 'A Stupid Jury's Work Completed', calling Williams 'the fiend'.

The Keowee Courier called his fate 'a just retribution' but regretted it was not inflicted 'under and by the law'; the Anderson Intelligencer called it 'a defiance of law' that public opinion would not condemn.
The Baptist Courier of Columbia, without disputing his guilt, wrote that lynching 'is nothing less than murder' and proposed a special law against it.
Papers outside the state ran the AP text under headlines such as 'Negro Hanged by a Mob', 'Mob Law in South Carolina' and 'An Objectionable Verdict Corrected'.
The Charlotte Home and Democrat used the case to call for jury reform, treating death as the 'righteous verdict' without endorsing the lynching itself.

conflicts.note: The Abbeville copy of the same News and Courier dispatch that reads 'eleven' in the Fairfield paper prints 14, so 14 looks like a typesetting error; most reports say 11.
South Carolina and Charleston sources give Linnie; 'Lizzie' appears in wire copies.
